items.followUp: Describe the structure and function of red blood cells.

rubric.why: Award for identifying the protective role of white blood cells against disease-causing organisms.
rubric.description: State that white blood cells defend the body against pathogens or infection.
rubric.how: 1 mark for defence/protection; 1 mark for linking this to pathogens or infection.

rubric.why: White blood cells protect the body through phagocytosis and by producing antibodies.
rubric.description: Explain one or both ways white blood cells fight infection: engulfing pathogens or producing antibodies.
rubric.how: 1 mark for phagocytosis/engulfing pathogens; 1 mark for antibody production by lymphocytes.

rubric.why: A nucleus is a characteristic feature that distinguishes white blood cells from red blood cells.
rubric.description: Mention that white blood cells have a nucleus.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that white blood cells contain a nucleus.

modelAnswer: White blood cells, also called leucocytes, are blood cells that protect the body against pathogens and disease.
They can move out of blood vessels and engulf pathogens by phagocytosis.
Some white blood cells, such as lymphocytes, produce antibodies that help destroy pathogens.
White blood cells have a nucleus and do not contain haemoglobin.

items.followUp: State four advantages of using scientific names for organisms.

rubric.why: A binomial name consists of two parts: the genus name and the specific name.
rubric.description: State that each scientific name has two parts: genus and species.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying both parts.

rubric.why: An internationally standardised name can be used by biologists everywhere.
rubric.description: Explain that the names are universal and used worldwide.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the idea of international or worldwide use.

rubric.why: Common names vary between places and languages, while a scientific name avoids this ambiguity.
rubric.description: Explain that binomial nomenclature avoids confusion caused by different local names.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking variable local names to confusion or ambiguity.

rubric.why: Scientific names help identify organisms consistently and place them in classification groups.
rubric.description: State that scientific names help with identification or classification of organisms.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a valid identification or classification benefit.

modelAnswer: Binomial nomenclature gives each organism a two-part scientific name: its genus name followed by its species name.
These names are standardised and used internationally, so scientists in different countries can refer to the same organism clearly.
Scientific names prevent confusion caused by different local or common names for an organism.
They also help identify and classify organisms according to their relationships.

items.followUp: Explain how fermentation by yeast is useful in making bread and alcoholic drinks.

rubric.why: Anaerobic respiration releases energy when oxygen is absent or insufficient.
rubric.description: Explain that anaerobic respiration releases energy without oxygen.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for absence or shortage of oxygen and 1 mark for release of energy.

rubric.why: Muscle cells can respire anaerobically during vigorous exercise, producing lactic acid.
rubric.description: Give the example of anaerobic respiration in muscles and its lactic acid product.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the muscle/lactic-acid example.

rubric.why: Yeast fermentation produces ethanol and carbon dioxide and has important uses.
rubric.description: State that yeast anaerobic respiration produces ethanol and carbon dioxide.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct products.

rubric.why: Carbon dioxide makes bread dough rise, while ethanol production is used in alcoholic drinks.
rubric.description: Give a practical use of yeast fermentation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct bread-making or alcoholic-drink use.

modelAnswer: Anaerobic respiration releases energy from glucose in the absence or shortage of oxygen.
During vigorous exercise, muscle cells may respire anaerobically and produce lactic acid.
In yeast, anaerobic respiration (fermentation) produces ethanol and carbon dioxide.
The carbon dioxide is used to make bread dough rise, and the ethanol is used to make alcoholic drinks.

items.followUp: Give two differences between plant and animal cells.

rubric.why: Prokaryotic cells lack a membrane-bound nucleus, while eukaryotic cells have one.
rubric.description: Compare the presence of a true nucleus.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct contrast.

rubric.why: Membrane-bound organelles are characteristic of eukaryotic cells and absent in prokaryotic cells.
rubric.description: Compare the presence of membrane-bound organelles.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct contrast.

rubric.why: Prokaryotic DNA is typically circular and lies in the nucleoid; eukaryotic DNA is organised into chromosomes in the nucleus.
rubric.description: Compare the form or location of genetic material.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct contrast.

rubric.why: Prokaryotic cells are generally smaller than eukaryotic cells.
rubric.description: Compare their typical size.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that prokaryotic cells are generally smaller.

modelAnswer: Prokaryotic cells do not have a membrane-bound nucleus; eukaryotic cells have a membrane-bound nucleus.
Prokaryotic cells lack membrane-bound organelles; eukaryotic cells contain them.
Prokaryotic cells have circular DNA in a nucleoid; eukaryotic DNA is organised into chromosomes in the nucleus.
Prokaryotic cells are generally smaller than eukaryotic cells.

items.followUp: Define polymers and give two examples of biological polymers.

rubric.why: Macromolecules are large molecules, often formed by joining many smaller molecules.
rubric.description: Define macromolecules as large molecules formed from smaller units.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the definition.

rubric.why: Examples include proteins, carbohydrates, lipids and nucleic acids.
rubric.description: Give two correct examples of macromolecules.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for any two valid examples.

modelAnswer: Macromolecules are large molecules, often formed by joining many smaller molecules.
Examples include proteins and carbohydrates.

items.followUp: Define community level and give an example.

rubric.why: A population consists of members of the same species living in a particular area.
rubric.description: Define population level using same species and area.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for both elements of the definition.

rubric.why: A suitable example names a population of one species in a particular place.
rubric.description: Give a valid example of a population.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for an example such as frogs of the same species in a pond.

modelAnswer: Population level is a group of individuals of the same species living in a particular area at a particular time.
For example, all the frogs of one species living in a pond form a population.

rubric.why: Parasitology is the branch of biology concerned with parasites.
rubric.description: Define parasitology.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that it is the study of parasites.

rubric.why: Pharmacology studies drugs and their effects on living organisms or the body.
rubric.description: Define pharmacology.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that it is the study of drugs, including their effects.

modelAnswer: Parasitology is the branch of biology that studies parasites.
Pharmacology is the branch of biology that studies drugs and their effects on the body.

items.followUp: Name the medicinal substance obtained from cinchona bark and state its use.

rubric.why: Quina quina is the common name used for the cinchona plant.
rubric.description: Identify quina quina as the cinchona plant.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the plant as cinchona/quina quina.

rubric.why: Cinchona bark provides quinine, a medicine used to treat malaria.
rubric.description: State that the plant yields quinine, used against malaria.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for quinine and its use in treating malaria.

modelAnswer: Quina quina is the cinchona plant, whose bark contains the medicinal substance quinine.
Quinine is used to treat malaria.
